presidents.name: Herbert Hoover
trivia: First president born west of the Mississippi River (West Branch, Iowa).
First president to have a telephone installed on the president’s desk in the Oval Office.
The stock market crashed in October 1929, months after he took office, beginning the Great Depression.
Made his name as a mining engineer and as the humanitarian who organized food relief for Europe after World War I.
Shantytowns of homeless Americans during the Depression were nicknamed “Hoovervilles.”
Learned Mandarin Chinese while working as an engineer in China around the Boxer Rebellion.
Won a huge victory in 1928, then lost a huge defeat to Franklin Roosevelt in 1932.
The Hoover Dam on the Colorado River was named for him (briefly renamed Boulder Dam under FDR, then Hoover again).
Orphaned as a child and raised by relatives, including years in Oregon.
Believed private charity and limited federal relief should lead the response; critics blamed that approach as unemployment soared.
Pub-trivia shorthand: Depression scapegoat—“Hoovervilles”; engineer/humanitarian before the crash.
quiz: Which president learned Mandarin while working as an engineer in China?

presidents.name: Franklin D. Roosevelt
trivia: Only president elected to four terms; the 22nd Amendment later limited presidents to two.
First sitting president to fly in an airplane (to a wartime conference).
First president to appear on television, at the 1939 New York World’s Fair RCA exhibit.
Created the New Deal programs that include Social Security, the FDIC, the SEC, and the TVA.
Led the United States through most of World War II until his death in April 1945.
Paralyzed by polio in 1921; he used a wheelchair in private while appearing to stand with braces and aid in public.
Calmed Depression-era listeners with radio “fireside chats” and said in his first inaugural that “the only thing we have to fear is fear itself.”
A distant cousin of Theodore Roosevelt; he married Eleanor Roosevelt, TR’s niece.
Appears on the U.S. dime.
In 1936 he won every state except Maine and Vermont.
Pub-trivia shorthand: New Deal / four terms / WWII; only president elected more than twice; on the dime.
quiz: Which sitting president was the first to fly in an airplane?

presidents.name: Harry S. Truman
trivia: First president whose inauguration was broadcast on national television (1949).
The middle initial “S” does not stand for a name—his parents disagreed on honoring which grandfather, so it stayed “S.”
Authorized the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945.
Announced the Truman Doctrine and backed the Marshall Plan to contain Soviet influence and rebuild Europe.
Desegregated the U.S. armed forces by executive order in 1948.
Kept a desk sign reading “The Buck Stops Here,” meaning final responsibility was his.
Defeated Thomas Dewey in 1948 despite the Chicago Daily Tribune’s wrong early headline “Dewey Defeats Truman.”
His men’s clothing store in Kansas City failed in the 1920s before he entered politics.
Fired General Douglas MacArthur in 1951 during the Korean War for publicly challenging civilian control.
Last president who never earned a college degree.
Pub-trivia shorthand: drops the atomic bombs; “Dewey Defeats Truman”; “The Buck Stops Here.”

presidents.name: Dwight D. Eisenhower
trivia: Only president who held five-star general rank (General of the Army).
First president to hold a televised news conference (1955).
First president to appear on color television.
As Supreme Allied Commander in Europe, planned and oversaw the D-Day invasion of Normandy (1944).
Signed the law creating the Interstate Highway System.
Sent the 101st Airborne to Little Rock, Arkansas, in 1957 to enforce school desegregation.
In his farewell address, warned Americans about unwarranted influence by the “military-industrial complex.”
Campaign buttons and ads used the slogan “I Like Ike,” from his nickname.
Both major parties tried to recruit him after World War II; he ran as a Republican.
Born in Denison, Texas, and raised in Abilene, Kansas.
Pub-trivia shorthand: D-Day general → president; Interstates; “I Like Ike”; warns about the military-industrial complex.

presidents.name: John F. Kennedy
trivia: First Catholic president, and at 43 the youngest person ever elected president.
First president elected after televised debates; his 1960 debates with Richard Nixon are credited with boosting TV’s role in campaigns.
Managed the October 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis, when the U.S. and Soviet Union came closest to nuclear war.
Committed the U.S. to landing a man on the Moon before 1970 in his “we choose to go to the Moon” Rice University speech.
Assassinated in Dallas on November 22, 1963; the Warren Commission concluded Lee Harvey Oswald acted alone.
In World War II he commanded PT-109; after a Japanese destroyer sank it, he swam injured crew members to safety.
His inaugural address includes the line “Ask not what your country can do for you—ask what you can do for your country.”
Created the Peace Corps by executive order in 1961.
Authorized the failed CIA-backed Bay of Pigs invasion of Cuba in April 1961.
Won a Pulitzer Prize for Profiles in Courage, a book about U.S. senators who took unpopular stands.
Pub-trivia shorthand: Camelot; Cuban Missile Crisis; Moon speech; assassinated in Dallas.

presidents.name: Lyndon B. Johnson
trivia: First president sworn into office aboard an airplane—Air Force One in Dallas after Kennedy’s assassination.
Passed Great Society laws including the Civil Rights Act (1964), Voting Rights Act (1965), Medicare, and Medicaid.
Dramatically increased U.S. troop levels in Vietnam; the war’s cost and casualties destroyed his popularity.
As Senate majority leader he was famous for the “Johnson Treatment”—leaning in close and pressuring colleagues until they agreed.
Announced in March 1968 that he would not run for another term.
Crushed Barry Goldwater in the 1964 Electoral College landslide.
First Lady Claudia “Lady Bird” Johnson led a highway beautification campaign against billboard clutter.
The photo of him taking the oath beside Jacqueline Kennedy, still in her bloodstained pink suit, is one of the most famous in U.S. history.
A towering Texas Democrat known for physical intimidation and dealmaking in small rooms.
Initials LBJ are grouped with FDR and JFK as the most familiar presidential monograms.
Pub-trivia shorthand: sworn in on Air Force One after JFK; Civil Rights / Medicare; Vietnam destroys him.

presidents.name: Richard Nixon
trivia: Only president to resign from office, on August 9, 1974, because of the Watergate scandal.
In 1972 became the first sitting president to visit the People’s Republic of China, opening U.S.–China relations.
Created the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) in 1970.
Ended direct U.S. combat involvement in Vietnam and signed the Paris Peace Accords (1973).
Won 49 states against George McGovern in 1972—one of the biggest landslides—before Watergate unraveled his presidency.
Lost the 1960 presidential race to John F. Kennedy and the 1962 California governor’s race, then won the presidency in 1968.
His 1952 “Checkers” speech, defending a campaign fund and mentioning his dog Checkers, saved his spot as Eisenhower’s running mate.
Told reporters in 1973, “I’m not a crook,” a line forever tied to Watergate.
One month after Nixon resigned, President Gerald Ford issued him a full pardon.
A widely repeated but unverified story says he unknowingly helped Louis Armstrong bring marijuana through customs.
Pub-trivia shorthand: only president to resign—Watergate; opens China; creates the EPA.
quiz: Which future president allegedly smuggled marijuana for Louis Armstrong?

presidents.name: Gerald Ford
trivia: Only president never elected as either president or vice president: Nixon appointed him VP under the 25th Amendment, then Nixon resigned.
Pardoned Richard Nixon for any federal crimes, a move that likely cost Ford the 1976 election.
Survived two assassination attempts in September 1975—by Lynette “Squeaky” Fromme and Sara Jane Moore—both in California.
Was a University of Michigan football center who received NFL offers from the Lions and Packers and turned them down for law school.
Born Leslie Lynch King Jr.; after his mother remarried, he was renamed Gerald Rudolph Ford Jr.
Became vice president in 1973 after Spiro Agnew resigned over a bribery scandal.
Chevy Chase’s Saturday Night Live sketches of Ford constantly falling made “clumsy president” a national joke.
First Lady Betty Ford spoke publicly about her breast cancer and later her addiction; the Betty Ford Center treatment facility is named for her.
Represented Grand Rapids, Michigan, in the House and became House Republican leader before the VP appointment.
Lost a close 1976 election to Jimmy Carter.
Pub-trivia shorthand: never elected president or VP; pardons Nixon; Michigan football guy / SNL pratfalls.
quiz: Which president was never elected as either president or vice president?

presidents.name: Jimmy Carter
trivia: First president born in a hospital (Wise Sanitarium in Plains, Georgia, 1924).
Former peanut farmer and Georgia governor who won in 1976 as a post-Watergate Washington outsider.
Brokered the 1978 Camp David Accords, the peace framework between Egypt’s Anwar Sadat and Israel’s Menachem Begin.
The Iran hostage crisis (1979–81), high inflation, and energy shortages sank his 1980 reelection bid against Ronald Reagan.
Won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2002 for Habitat for Humanity work and international conflict mediation after leaving office.
Lived longer than any other U.S. president.
Graduated from the Naval Academy and served as a nuclear submarine officer under Admiral Hyman Rickover.
Installed solar water-heating panels on the White House roof during the energy crisis.
In retirement he became famous for personally helping build Habitat for Humanity houses.
His marriage to Rosalynn Carter lasted more than 75 years—the longest of any presidential couple.
Pub-trivia shorthand: peanut farmer; Camp David Accords; Iran hostages; Habitat-for-Humanity retirement.

presidents.name: Ronald Reagan
trivia: First Hollywood film actor elected president; he had also been president of the Screen Actors Guild.
At 69, he was the oldest person elected president at the time (later surpassed by Trump and Biden).
Survived an assassination attempt by John Hinckley Jr. outside a Washington hotel in March 1981.
In 1987 in West Berlin he challenged Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev: “Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!”
Pushed major income-tax cuts, deregulation, and a defense buildup; supporters credit him with helping end the Cold War.
Nicknamed the “Great Communicator” for clear TV-era speeches.
Starred in the 1951 comedy Bedtime for Bonzo opposite a chimpanzee—a movie opponents never stopped mentioning.
Served two terms as governor of California (1967–1975) before the presidency.
The Iran-Contra affair revealed secret arms sales to Iran and diversion of funds to Nicaraguan Contras during his second term.
After being shot, he joked to the surgeons, “Please tell me you’re all Republicans.”
Pub-trivia shorthand: Hollywood actor president; “tear down this wall”; survives Hinckley shooting.
